finding: In the start week and the week after, mules pay out within 24 h an amount worth 80-100% of a payment they have just received, which normal accounts rarely do; it works the same for real customers and fakes.
evidence: Section 3, match_share at the start week: all 0.87 (0.85-0.88), fake 0.87 (0.85-0.88), real 0.88 (0.86-0.90) (witting 0.88 (0.85-0.91), unwitting 0.87 (0.84-0.90)); week after real 0.84 (0.81-0.87); real inside income bands 0.88 (0.85-0.90), inside age bands 0.88 (0.85-0.90); real inside quintiles of out_24h_share_wk 0.75 (0.71-0.79) and of out_1h_share_wk 0.78 (0.74-0.82); a matched payment occurs in 1.3% of normal weeks vs 59% / 57% of witting / unwitting start weeks; week before the start real 0.50 (0.46-0.54).
sim_setting: laundering.holder_keeps [0, 0.10] (amount in = pieces / (1 - keep) in src/sim/laundering.py) with laundering.out_pieces_mean 2.0 and laundering.split_max_n_in 4; normal transfers out are drawn independently of money in (src/sim/normal.py)
artefact: partly: forwarding minus a small commission is documented (Europol/FBI), but the 0-10% cut is an assumption and normal accounts never pass on a received amount by design, so the gap is likely wider than in a real bank
feature_sketch: match_share_wk = money paid out (not card) within 24 h of the latest payment in and worth 80-100% of it / money in this week, plus its 4-week sum version

finding: In the start week, a mule's largest single payment out is bigger than anything the account paid out before; it holds for real customers with long normal histories, not only for newly opened fake accounts.
evidence: Section 4, max_out_vs_hist (raw rows, card left out) at the start week: all 0.84 (0.82-0.86), fake 0.85 (0.83-0.87), real 0.81 (0.77-0.86) (witting 0.83 (0.77-0.88), unwitting 0.80 (0.72-0.86)); week after real 0.79 (0.74-0.83); real inside income bands 0.81 (0.77-0.85), inside age bands 0.81 (0.77-0.86), inside quintiles of money_out_wk 0.77 (0.72-0.81); store-only version real 0.79 (0.75-0.84), inside quintiles of max_out_wk 0.74 (0.68-0.79); week before the start real 0.54 (0.49-0.59).
sim_setting: laundering.out_transfer_mean 532 x laundering.shapes amount_rel with laundering.piece_sigma 0.6, against normal one-off transfers sized from income (normal.non_card_value_weights, normal.amount_sigma 0.6)
artefact: partly: mules moving bigger sums than their usual is real (the bank's R6 'sudden change' rule looks for it), but the size of the gap rests on modelling spreads and on normal amounts scaling with income only
feature_sketch: max_out_vs_hist = max_out_wk / largest max_out_wk in weeks 0..w-1 (NaN until an earlier week has money out); a raw version that leaves out the weekly card row was a little stronger

finding: Mules pay the same payee two or more times within one week, from the start week to two weeks after, which almost no normal account ever does.
evidence: Section 5: over all 164,819 accounts of months 0-4 and weeks 0-77, 2 normal accounts ever have such a week vs 109 of 135 real mules (79 already in the start week) and 281 of 320 fakes; rep_payee_max at the start week all 0.81 (0.79-0.83), fake 0.82 (0.79-0.85), real 0.79 (0.75-0.83) (witting 0.78 (0.72-0.83), unwitting 0.80 (0.73-0.86)); real inside quintiles of n_payees_wk 0.79 (0.74-0.83); week before the start real 0.50 (0.49-0.51).
sim_setting: src/sim/normal.py generate_normal: every one-off normal transfer goes to a new random payee (ext_ids) and Direct Debits / standing orders are monthly; laundering.shapes recipients (1 receiver in 6 of 15 shapes)
artefact: yes: real customers often pay the same person or their own savings account several times a week, but the simulator never lets a normal account repeat a payee within a week, so this is a near-perfect label here that would not carry over to a real bank
feature_sketch: rep_payee_max_wk = most payments to one payee (not cash, not card) this week; do not trial, recorded so nobody tries it again

finding: In the start week, real-customer mules send a bigger share of the week's money out to other accounts inside the bank than normal accounts do, much more clearly than fakes; the store's cumulative share dilutes it.
evidence: Section 6, internal_out_share_wk at the start week: all 0.66 (0.64-0.68), fake 0.63 (0.60-0.65), real 0.75 (0.70-0.79) (witting 0.72 (0.65-0.79), unwitting 0.77 (0.70-0.83)); week after real 0.72 (0.68-0.77); real inside income bands 0.75 (0.70-0.79), inside age bands 0.75 (0.70-0.79), inside quintiles of internal_out_share_cum 0.74 (0.70-0.78) and of out_1h_share_wk 0.74 (0.70-0.79); any internal money out in 13% of normal weeks vs 53% / 61% of witting / unwitting start weeks; week before the start real 0.50 (0.48-0.53); rebuilt exactly from store columns (largest difference 7e-15).
sim_setting: networks.internal_pieces_share 0.5 and laundering.layered_internal_multiplier 2 (a piece goes to the next network member only once it has started, src/sim/laundering.py); chains ordered so money flows to members who started earlier (src/sim/accounts.py); normal.internal_share_of_transfers 0.10
artefact: partly: mule networks are real (Vocalink) but how many hops stay inside one bank is a modelling value, and real mules show it more than fakes because the simulator passes money only to members who started earlier, which favours late-starting real customers
feature_sketch: internal_out_share_wk = (internal_out_share_cum x money_out_cum - the same product last week) / money_out_wk, plus a 4-week version
